attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post, not a quote.

semantics.note: 'It' plausibly means frustration with AI or the backlash. Either way it states a present condition: both parties are divided over AI.

contract.note: Reading 'splitting' as visible internal disagreement within US Democrats and Republicans over AI policy or infrastructure is an ordinary reading. The window is chosen by the evaluator but sensible. It sets no national-scale threshold, which is generous but not stretched.

evidence.note: Dated Apr 29, 2026, inside the window. Maine Democratic legislators publicly opposed Democratic Gov. Mills's veto of a data-center pause. This is a Democratic split over AI infrastructure. It is less clear on the Republican side.
AP, Apr 19, 2026. Utah Republicans Fiefia and McCay take opposing positions on state AI safeguards, and Fiefia breaks with the Trump administration. This is a clear Republican split.

reviews.rationale: Records from inside the window name members of each party on opposite sides of AI-related policy. Democrats split over Maine's data-center pause, and Republicans split over Utah AI regulation and Trump's stance. That meets the contract's plain reading of 'splitting'. Nothing shows the positions were misattributed. The cases are state-level, but the claim gave no threshold for scale.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Two parts: the backlash is growing, and new signs appear near-daily. 'I see' describes his own exposure, and the drafter reasonably turns it into a claim about public opposition.

contract.note: It scores growing opposition plus a frequent stream of examples, and does not require one every day. That is an ordinary reading. The window is chosen by the evaluator, and scope and measure are unspecified, which the contract flags.

evidence.note: Gallup poll of Gen Z (ages 14–29), fieldwork Feb–Mar 2026, before the window. It shows anger at AI rising, but this population and period cannot establish the claim.
Chalkbeat, May 1, 2026. Large parent opposition to AI in NYC schools, and an AI-focused school proposal withdrawn. One substantial example, not a trend or near-daily stream.

reviews.rationale: The packet has one dated opposition event inside the window and one earlier Gen Z poll showing more anger. Neither shows a general-public trend or a frequent stream of distinct events, and the packet itself notes these gaps. Nothing shows the backlash declining. The evidence does not settle the claim either way.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence, offered as his theory.

semantics.note: It attributes some of the preceding harms to technical unreliability and some to political/economic failures such as lacking regulation. The 'some' scope is preserved.

contract.note: The plain reading asks whether model failures contributed to some harms and inadequate governance contributed to others. That is fair. It does not hold 'utter lack' to a literal no-laws test.

evidence.note: Mata v. Avianca opinion (June 2023, inside the period). ChatGPT produced fake cases, causing harm. This supports technical unreliability as a contributor, though the court puts responsibility on the lawyers.

A legislator's office announces California SB 243 chatbot safeguards, effective Jan 2026. Labeled a company disclosure, but it is an official announcement. It neither proves nor refutes inadequate regulation.

reviews.rationale: The technical part has support: a court record shows harm from LLM fabrication. The packet has no causal evidence that missing or ineffective regulation contributed to particular harms. SB 243 only shows some safeguards existed, which does not refute the claim. The support condition needs both parts, and nothing contradicts either, so the claim stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words, adapted from his own earlier post.

semantics.note: The full list of harms is kept, and the data-center clause stays a risk, not an outcome.

contract.note: Reading it as a material contribution to each harm, not the sole cause, assessed component by component, is fair and ordinary. A conjunction this broad is demanding, but that comes from the speaker's own wording.

evidence.note: FBI IC3 advisory, Dec 2024: generative AI makes fraud, phishing, impersonation and fake sexual imagery more scalable. Qualitative, with no measured increase.
Randomized trial in one Turkish high school: unrestricted GPT cut unaided exam performance by 17%, and guardrails removed the harm. Partial support only. It does not show aggregate harm to education.
International AI Safety Report 2026: chatbots may amplify delusions in vulnerable users, but there is no clear causal evidence. This is a limitation, not a refutation.

BIS Bulletin, Jan 2026: AI financing is shifting to debt, and macro risks look moderate. This partly bears on leverage risk but does not establish over-leverage or recession risk at the claimed scale.

reviews.rationale: Some components get partial support: cybercrime, impersonation and phishing, deepfake imagery, and local education harm. Delusions and leverage risk are left uncertain. Surveillance, disinformation, employment bias, economic disparity, slop and environmental harm have no decisive evidence. No component is refuted. The contract needs every component, so the bundle stays unresolved.
